newsitem.title: DUBAI: UAE law on illegal aliens leaves labour vacuum.
newsitem.headline: UAE law on illegal aliens leaves labour vacuum.

text.p: The last among tens of thousands of illegal foreign workers taking advantage of a government amnesty made their way out of the United Arab Emirates on Thursday, one day before tough new labour laws take effect.

Diplomats estimate 200,000 illegal workers have flooded out of the oil-rich state -- which they say represents about 15 to 20 percent of the workforce -- to avoid penalties such as jail terms, fines and deportation when a three-month amnesty for unlawful labourers ends and the law comes into force on Friday.
The UAE says the law will curb the growing number of illegal aliens, who it says pose a security threat to the country.
But businesses and residents say they are now struggling to cope with the mass exodus of labour and economists expect a short-term slowdown in business activity.

"Some 200,000 plus people have left the UAE, which represents about 15 to 20 percent of the workforce," a Western diplomat told Reuters. "The government expected 40,000 to 50,000 people to leave. This exceeded their wildest expectations."

In the latest official figures, the government said last week more than 160,000 illegal workers had left the UAE, where foreigners -- mostly from the Indian subcontinent and southeast Asia -- make up 75-80 percent of the 2.4 million population.
Business people say the outflow has caused a labour vacuum in the Gulf state, where many companies rely on cheap, unskilled workers to get jobs done quickly and at a low cost.

Many professionals also complain they have lost baby-sitters and household help who enabled them and their spouses to work. Some worry the law may force many women to give up their jobs. It says the legislation will also crack down on an abundance of visa scam operations.

Many foreign workers come to the UAE legally, but break the law by staying on when their visas expire or by absconding from their sponsors. The practices have always been illegal, but the new law imposes tougher penalties.
Interior Minister Lieutenant-General Mohammed Said al-Badi said the measures aimed at "rectifying the imbalance in the population and targeted all nationalities, not a specific one".
But diplomats say the government may have bitten off more than it could chew.
"This isn't the way to solve the problem of the population imbalance. But the UAE is young and inexperienced and this is part of a learning process," one Western diplomat said.
Particularly hard-hit by the new law is the UAE's booming construction sector, and industry sources said the labour shortage meant many firms could not finish projects on time.
"This law will have a critical impact on the construction industry," a Western businessman in Dubai said. "Companies are scrambling to find labour."
The $6 billion construction industry contributes about 10 percent to the UAE's gross domestic product.
But despite the labour shortages and fears of an economic downturn, diplomats and business executives predict the long-term economic impact of the new law will be limited.
"In the next six to eight months it is going to be painful to replace these workers," one economic analyst said.

"But ultimately the companies will get the labour back, and legally this time. That will make the cost of labour more expensive, but companies will deal by streamlining operations and raising labour efficiency," he said.
